page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.hfg5.2xlarge is a high-clock-speed computing instance built on the KVM hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. The server delivers 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 4 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 6149 processor operating at a nominal base frequency of 3.1 GHz. Supported instruction extensions include AVX, AVX-512F, and AES. Memory allocation is set at 32.0 GB, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. The instance comes without local storage, requiring network-attached disks, and features a baseline network throughput of 2 Gbps without bundled GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark results present a profile defined by moderate multithreaded capacity alongside modest single-core throughput. In synthetic CPU assessments, the instance generated a multi-core score of 7,202.07 in stress-ng and 8,278.74 in PassMark, placing both metrics in the average tier. Single-core evaluations, including Geekbench at 1,088.0 and stress-ng at 1,355.18, fell into the lower quartile. Memory throughput under large 256 MB block read operations reached 38.36 GB/sec, reflecting lower-tier uncached memory performance, while small-block cached read speed remained consistent at 402.34 GB/sec.

Application and compilation tasks reflect the instance's balanced core structure. The server achieved an average Geekbench Clang compilation rating of 6,738.0 and sustained 7.09 million operations per second in Redis SET operations. However, throughput constraints appear in high-throughput network and data operations, where static web serving hit 4.68 GB/sec and PassMark database operations scored 2,430.26. Natural language processing workloads execute acceptably on small 135M parameter models (94.92 tokens/sec generation), but performance degrades substantially to 4.8 tokens/sec on 7B models.

From an architectural standpoint, ecs.hfg5.2xlarge delivers predictable dedicated compute allocation with standard memory density. The absence of local disk drives requires external block storage planning, and the 2 Gbps network baseline limits extreme data transfer scenarios. It is primarily suitable for routine application backends, development compilation environments, small in-memory caches, and enterprise batch workers with steady multithreaded demands.
